newsitem.title: USA: Big automakers plan to slow air bags in Canada.
newsitem.headline: Big automakers plan to slow air bags in Canada.

text.p: Detroit's Big Three automakers plan to warn consumers about potential dangers from air bags and reduce the power of the safety devices in Canada, an industry group said Friday.

Since U.S. regulators said at the end of 1992 that air bags would be required in all new cars by next September, the devices have saved about 1,100 lives but also killed 28 children and 19 adults, Andrew Card, president of the American Automobile Manufacturers Association, said.
"The good news is that air bags work, air bags have saved lives," he told a media briefing. "We also know, unfortunately, that air bags have caused deaths."
Automakers have been installing the bags before the regulators' deadline.

Air bags typically inflate at about 200 miles an hour and will be "de-powered" in Canada by about 25 percent, he said. The first cars with the lower-power air bags should hit the roads in Canada within six months, Card said.
The trade association, which represents Chrysler, Ford and General Motors, said the force with which air bags inflate cannot be reduced in the United States without regulatory changes.

So for now, in the United States the three automakers will send letters to owners of cars with passenger-side air bags and include additional warning labels in all new vehicles outlining risks associated with air bags as well as guidelines for proper use.
One of the main messages the carmakers want to get across is that children should always ride in the back seat and not in the front on the passenger side.
Small adults and elderly people also need to be cautious, and all occupants should sit at least 12 inches from the dashboard and always wear seat and shoulder belts, Card said.
Air bag deaths are usually caused when someone is hit by the deploying bag, rather than from suffocation.
Henry Jasny, chief counsel at Advocates for Highway and Auto Safety, said the consumer group considers air bags safe and was trying to spread the message about child safety.
The group also advocates a label on the dashboard warning consumers that air bags can be dangerous for children in the front seat or anyone who sits too close.
Reducing the force of the air bag, as the automakers will do in Canada, would only be a positive step if it would reduce harm to children and maintain safety for adult drivers, Jasny said.

The auto group's Card said even with lower-powered air bags, children 12 and under should not travel in the front seat. Lessening the force of the device would not compromise the safety it provides, he said.

"The net safety benefit of de-powering is real," Card said. "People should know how to use their cars when they're equipped with air bags. Always wear your safety belt, sit as far back from the steering wheel or the dashboard as you can," he said.
"That's the right way to respect an air bag, and air bags demand respect," Card said.
Reducing the force of air bags by removing some of the propellant was not expected to have much impact on prices, Card said.
"It's not a terribly expensive process, yes there will be an expense to the industry but I don't expect that it would impact the price of a vehicle," he said.
